lessons.title: Synthesis — sentences worth saying
lessons.gloss: synthesis — the first sentences in this book long enough to be worth saying, and why length is not the same as difficulty

segments.text: Until this rung, every sentence you could build had one verb in it. Count the verbs in the next one.
— ¿Tienes el libro que compré? — Sí. Lo que no tengo es la comida que haces.
Read the second line again. It has three verbs in it, and you can build every piece of it:
lo que no tengo — the thing I do not have (a noun-shaped hole).
la comida que haces — the meal you make (a noun with a sentence hung off it).
Nothing in that sentence is new. What is new is that the pieces are allowed to sit inside each other.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: length is not difficulty

segments.text: Long sentences look like an increase in difficulty and are not.

A relative clause does not add grammar. It adds a slot where a whole sentence can go, and you fill it with the same Spanish you were already making. Two short sentences become one long one, and the only new thing is the joint.

That is why this is the last structural rung a beginner's course owes you. Not because nothing is left, but because from here the growth is more of what you have, arranged more deeply. What remains genuinely hard is vocabulary and hearing speed, and both are time.

segments.instruction: the long sentence broken into its three pieces, then whole

segments.prompt: Ask whether somebody has the book you bought.

feedback.correct: The que English would have dropped.

segments.prompt: Say the thing I do not have.
Say what I do not have is the meal you make.
acceptedResponses: lo que no tengo es la comida que haces
lo que no tengo es la comida que haces.

feedback.correct: Three verbs, and every piece was already yours.
feedback.incorrect: Lo que no tengo es la comida que haces.

segments.prompt: Why is a long sentence not harder than the short ones it is made of?
acceptedResponses: the clause only adds a slot, not new grammar
it is the same spanish arranged inside itself

feedback.correct: The only new thing is the joint.
feedback.incorrect: A relative clause adds a slot where a sentence can go — not new grammar.

segments.text: How many verbs can one sentence hold now? (As many as you can join.) What does a relative clause actually add? (A slot, not new grammar.) And what is genuinely hard from here? (Vocabulary and hearing speed — both of which are time.)
